subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Thursday, after closing.
Three weeks in, and Pema still apologises for everything. Today a customer's coffee order got mixed up at the bakery counter and the woman started raising her voice. Pema said sorry, remade it, and slipped a small butter biscuit on the saucer with a note: 'for the wait'. The woman left smiling.
Last week I told Pema 'good job!' after the lunch rush and got a shrug. 'You're just being nice, Ira.' Fair. It was vague.
So today, while we wiped the counters, I was specific. 'The mix-up. You stayed calm, you fixed it fast, and the note turned an angry customer into a regular. I saw her book a cake order on her way out.'
Pema stopped wiping. 'She did?' Then, quietly, 'I didn't know if the biscuit was allowed.'
'It was the best part.'
Later I saw her write something on a sticky note and put it in her apron pocket.

qa.q: What did Pema put on the saucer for the angry customer?
qa.a: Pema slipped a small butter biscuit on the saucer with a note: 'for the wait'.

qa.q: Why did Pema shrug off Ira's 'good job!' the week before?
qa.a: Pema doubted her own work and thought Ira was just being nice, so vague praise felt empty.

qa.q: Why did Ira's praise land better today?
qa.a: Ira named exactly what Pema did well and its result, which gave Pema facts her doubting mind could actually believe.

qa.q: What might Pema's sticky note in her apron pocket suggest about how she took the praise?
qa.a: It suggests she valued it enough to keep it, perhaps as proof to look at the next time she doubts herself 🙂

grounding: It shows a supervisor who gives specific, honest praise to a doubting newcomer after noticing that vague praise was brushed off.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
At the cooperative bank branch in the kasba, the pension-day queue stretched out to the tea stall. Lokesh, the branch manager, watched his new clerk, Siddharth, deal with old Tukaram kaka, who was shouting that his pension had been stolen.
Siddharth didn't shout back. He pulled up the passbook, found that the amount had gone into an old account, explained it slowly in Marathi, and walked kaka to the next counter to fix it.
Afterwards Lokesh said, "Good job." Siddharth shrugged. "Anyone could have done it. I still don't know half the software."
The words had bounced straight off. At closing time Lokesh tried again. "This morning, three things you did right. You didn't argue with kaka. You checked the old account before blaming anyone. And you walked him over yourself instead of pointing."
Siddharth looked at the floor, then up. "The old account... yes, I did think of that." He wrote something in the back of his register.

qa.q: Where had Tukaram kaka's pension gone?
qa.a: Into an old account.

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel when Siddharth shrugged off 'good job'?
qa.a: He felt concerned that vague praise had bounced off a doubting newcomer, and decided to be specific.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's second attempt at praise land?
qa.a: It named three concrete actions Siddharth took, facts the doubting mind could not easily dismiss as kindness.

qa.q: What might Siddharth be feeling when he writes in the back of his register?
qa.a: He may feel quietly encouraged, holding on to concrete evidence that he handled the crisis well.

grounding: A small-town bank manager sees vague praise fail with a doubting new clerk and then names exactly what he did well.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
In Valentina's third week at the café in Porto, the espresso machine broke at 8 a.m. on a Saturday. Dalia, the manager, was stuck on the phone with the repair company and watched from the back.
Valentina didn't freeze. She put a sign on the counter, switched everyone to filter coffee and tea, handed free custard tarts to the grumpiest part of the queue, and kept the line moving with a joke about the machine needing a holiday.
When it was over she came to Dalia with red cheeks. "I'm sorry. I probably made a mess. I'm still so slow."
Dalia had told her "You're doing great" twice that week, and both times Valentina had only nodded. This time Dalia was specific. "You switched the menu within two minutes. You gave tarts to the people most likely to complain. Not one customer walked out. That was a manager's call."
Valentina blinked. "Not one?"
"I counted."

qa.q: What did Valentina switch everyone to?
qa.a: Filter coffee and tea.

qa.q: What was Dalia thinking when she chose to be specific this time?
qa.a: Dalia felt frustrated that 'you're doing great' had not reached Valentina, and hoped concrete facts would reassure her.

qa.q: What made Dalia's feedback something Valentina could accept?
qa.a: It listed exact actions and one fact, that not one customer walked out, which is harder to dismiss than general praise.

qa.q: What is Valentina feeling when she apologises with red cheeks?
qa.a: She feels anxious and embarrassed, sure she made a mess, even though she handled the crisis well.

grounding: A café manager notices a doubting new hire discount vague praise and gives specific, honest feedback on what she did well.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
In the women's ward of the district hospital, Binita, the nurse in charge, had noticed that Zubin, the new nursing assistant, said "sorry" about twenty times a shift.
On Tuesday night an elderly patient in bed 12 became confused and tried to pull out her drip. Zubin got there first. He held her hand, spoke softly to her about her grandchildren, kept the drip in place and pressed the call bell without leaving her side. By the time Binita arrived, the patient was calm.
At handover he said, "Sorry, I should have noticed earlier."
Binita had already learned that "well done" slid off him like water. So she said, "You stayed with her instead of running for help. You kept the line safe. You called me without letting go. That's exactly the order I'd want."
Zubin looked at her as if checking she meant it. Then he nodded slowly and, for once, didn't say sorry.

qa.q: Which bed was the confused patient in?
qa.a: Bed 12.

qa.q: What had Binita noticed about Zubin before Tuesday, and how did it make her feel?
qa.a: She was concerned that he apologised constantly, a sign of self-doubt that made plain 'well done' slide off him.

qa.q: Why is Binita's feedback at handover effective?
qa.a: She named the exact steps Zubin took and their order, giving his doubting mind facts he could accept.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when he doesn't say sorry for once?
qa.a: He probably feels surprised and a little more confident, believing for a moment that he did the right thing.

grounding: A senior nurse notices a new assistant's constant apologies and gives specific, honest praise naming what he did well.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Subject: Your first month, specifically
Hi Deepak,
In our check-in yesterday you said you "just got lucky" with the vendor report. I didn't argue then, but I want to put this in writing, because I don't think it was luck.
Three things you did:
1. You noticed the two suppliers were using different units and converted them before anyone else caught it. That saved us a wrong order.
2. Your summary on page one was four lines. Our director read it in the lift and forwarded it without edits. That almost never happens.
3. When you weren't sure about the warehouse codes, you asked Meera instead of guessing.
I know a new job makes everyone feel like a fake; I felt it for a year. But these are facts, not compliments. Keep this email, and read it again the next time you think you don't belong here.
Payal

qa.q: What did Deepak notice about the two suppliers?
qa.a: That they were using different units, which Deepak converted before anyone else caught it.

qa.q: Why did Payal decide to put the praise in writing?
qa.a: Payal was concerned that Deepak was dismissing real work as luck and, having felt like a fake in a new job once, wanted to give facts Deepak could keep.

qa.q: Why is Payal's praise more likely to be believed than a quick "good job"?
qa.a: It names specific actions and results, like the unit conversion and the four-line summary, which a doubting mind cannot easily dismiss.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel reading the email?
qa.a: Deepak may feel surprised and reassured, seeing concrete proof that the good result was not luck.

grounding: Shows a manager giving a doubting newcomer specific, honest praise that names exactly what was done, so it cannot be brushed off as vague.
